entries.title: Habits take time to become automatic, and one missed day doesn't break them
entries.citation: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009.
entries.finding: Automaticity rose along a curve and leveled off after a median of 66 days (range 18–254). Missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation.
entries.use: the 66-day growth arc; "never miss twice" instead of a streak that resets to zero.

entries.title: "If-then" plans improve follow-through
entries.citation: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119.
entries.finding: Across 94 independent tests, forming implementation intentions ("when situation X, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment (d = .65).
entries.use: every habit is written as "After I [cue], I will [action] at [place/time]."

entries.title: Habits are triggered by stable context cues
entries.citation: Wood, W., & Neal, D. T. (2007). A new look at habits and the habit–goal interface. Psychological Review, 114(4), 843–863.
entries.finding: Habits are cued by context (time, place, preceding action), not by goals or intentions alone.
entries.use: asking for a cue and a place, and reminding at that time.

entries.title: Start tiny and anchor to an existing routine
entries.citation: Fogg, B. J. (2019). Tiny Habits: The Small Changes That Change Everything. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt.
entries.use: design input for "start tiny, grow later" and anchoring. Not a marketing claim on its own; the anchoring part is supported by HAB-2 and HAB-3.

entries.title: Tracking progress helps people reach goals, more so when recorded and shared
entries.citation: Harkin, B., Webb, T. L., Chang, B. P. I., Prestwich, A., Conner, M., Kellar, I., Benn, Y., & Sheeran, P. (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin, 142(2), 198–229.
entries.finding: Prompting people to monitor progress improved goal attainment. Effects were larger when progress was physically recorded and when it was reported to others or made public.
entries.use: logging in every tracker; the feed and weekly review.

entries.title: Reminders and prompts help health behaviors
entries.citation: Fry, J. P., & Neff, R. A. (2009). Periodic prompts and reminders in health promotion and health behavior interventions: Systematic review. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 11(2), e16.
entries.finding: Most included studies found that periodic prompts had a positive effect on behavior.
entries.use: reminders at the time the user chose in their plan.

entries.title: A shared language for behavior change techniques
entries.citation: Michie, S., Richardson, M., Johnston, M., Abraham, C., Francis, J., Hardeman, W., Eccles, M. P., Cane, J., & Wood, C. E. (2013). The behavior change technique taxonomy (v1) of 93 hierarchically clustered techniques. Annals of Behavioral Medicine, 46(1), 81–95.
entries.use: tagging each Grove mechanic with the technique it implements (goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, prompts/cues, social support, feedback on behavior).

entries.title: Autonomy, competence and relatedness drive lasting motivation
entries.citation: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68–78.
entries.use: coach tone (supportive, never shaming), letting users choose their goals and display mode, showing competence through progress, the feed for relatedness.

entries.title: Gamification works for some people in some contexts
entries.citation: Hamari, J., Koivisto, J., & Sarsa, H. (2014). Does gamification work? A literature review of empirical studies on gamification. Proceedings of the 47th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, 3025–3034.
entries.finding: Mostly positive effects, but dependent on context and the user.
entries.use: Game mode is optional, not the default for everyone.

entries.title: Testing yourself beats rereading
entries.citation: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
entries.finding: Retrieval practice produced better retention on delayed tests than restudying.
entries.use: recall questions generated from the user's own book notes.

entries.title: Spacing out review improves long-term memory
entries.citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.
entries.use: scheduling recall questions over days and weeks after a reading session.

entries.title: Practice testing and spaced practice are the most useful study techniques
entries.citation: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.
entries.finding: Of ten common techniques, practice testing and distributed practice were rated high utility; highlighting and rereading were rated low.
entries.use: why Books asks questions instead of just storing highlights.

entries.title: How much activity adults need
entries.citation: Bull, F. C., et al. (2020). World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 54(24), 1451–1462.
entries.finding: Adults: 150–300 minutes of moderate (or 75–150 vigorous) aerobic activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days.
entries.use: the weekly activity ring and strength-day target.

entries.title: Progressive overload for strength
entries.citation: American College of Sports Medicine. (2009). Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 41(3), 687–708.
entries.finding: Gradually increase training stimulus; for novices, moderate loads for about 8–12 repetitions, and increase load when the target repetitions can be exceeded.
entries.use: "time to add weight" suggestions in Training.

entries.title: Protein intake for people who strength train
entries.citation: Morton, R. W., et al. (2018). A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 52(6), 376–384.
entries.finding: Benefits to muscle mass leveled off at about 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day.
entries.use: the optional protein target. Not medical advice.

entries.title: Daily weighing, viewed as a trend, supports weight management
entries.citation: Steinberg, D. M., Bennett, G. G., Askew, S., & Tate, D. F. (2015). Weighing every day matters: Daily weighing improves weight loss and adoption of weight control behaviors. *Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 115*(4), 511–518.
entries.use: weight logging with a 7-day average trend line.

entries.title: Aerobic exercise and the brain
entries.citation: Erickson, K. I., et al. (2011). Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(7), 3017–3022.
entries.finding: In older adults, a year of aerobic exercise increased hippocampal volume and improved memory compared with stretching.
entries.use: explaining how physical and cognitive growth connect. Word carefully: older adults, one trial.

entries.title: Couch to 5K
entries.citation: NHS. Couch to 5K running plan (9 weeks, three runs per week, run/walk intervals).
entries.use: structure for the beginner running plan. Widely used public program, not a trial.

entries.title: Adults need 7 or more hours of sleep
entries.citation: Watson, N. F., et al. (2015). Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: A joint consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society. Sleep, 38(6), 843–844.
entries.use: the sleep habit template's default target.

entries.title: Meditation programs and well-being
entries.citation: Goyal, M., et al. (2014). Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: A systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(3), 357–368.
entries.finding: Moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation programs improve anxiety, depression and pain.
entries.use: the meditation habit template. Do not claim it treats any condition.

entries.title: Doing it with others helps people stick with it
entries.citation: Wing, R. R., & Jeffery, R. W. (1999). Benefits of recruiting participants with friends and increasing social support for weight loss and maintenance. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 67(1), 132–138.
entries.finding: People who joined with friends and received social support were more likely to complete the program and keep the weight off.
entries.use: followers, the feed, cheering on milestones.
